Al Ain Oasis: Al Ain Oasis (Arabic: واحة العين, "Oasis of the Spring") is the largest oasis in the city of Al Ain, in the Eastern Region of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. It is in the Al Mutawa'a District in central Al Ain, east of the Al Jahili District.

Al Ain Oasis: Al Ain Oasis has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011. It opened to the public in 2016 with an educational Eco-Centre and an extensive system of shaded pathways that wind through some 147,000 date palms.
Al Ain Oasis: Al Ain Oasis has around 100 varieties of plants, with widespread plantations that are also working farms.
Al Ain Oasis: Al Ain Oasis dates back more than 4,000 years.

Al Ain Oasis: The oasis is known for its underground irrigation system (falaj or qanat), which brings water from boreholes to water farms and palm trees. The falaj is an ancient system dating back thousands of years and is used widely in Oman, the UAE, India, Iran and other countries.
Al Ain Oasis: Al Ain Oasis has various facilities including the Eco-Centre, Oasis Garden, Miniature Oasis and Falaj Exhibition.

Al Ain Oasis: The Eco-Centre at Al Ain Oasis is an eco-friendly building which acts as a time machine, taking visitors from the present back into the past. It has interactive screens and educational activities.
Al Ain Oasis: The Oasis Garden at Al Ain Oasis is divided into three sections, each displaying plants found in traditional oasis farms.

Al Ain Oasis: The Miniature Oasis at Al Ain Oasis is a scale model of the oasis which illustrates how and why it was built. Visitors can see the distribution of water from the aflaj irrigation channels and the forts built for protection that surround the oasis.
Al Ain Oasis: Next to Al Ain Oasis are the Al Ain National Museum and Sultan Fort to the east, and the Sheikh Zayed Palace Museum (Al Ain Palace Museum, currently closed for renovation) to the west.

Al Jahili Fort: Al Jahili Fort's inner square fort was built in the 1890s by Sheikh Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan, also known as Zayed the First or Zayed the Great, who ruled Abu Dhabi from 1855 to 1909. An inscription over the south gate shows this date. Construction is reported to have begun around 1891.
Al Jahili Fort: Al Jahili Fort was built in Al Jahili Oasis, in a strategic spot with water sources and agricultural land, to protect the date palm farmers.
Al Jahili Fort: Al Jahili Fort stands at the centre of Al Ain. It has come to symbolize the traditional architecture and cultural heritage of Abu Dhabi.

Al Jahili Fort: The Al Jahili Fort complex has a round watchtower, a square fort with defensive towers at its corners, two large walled enclosures and a mosque outside the walls. The parts added in the 1980s use the same traditional mudbrick walls with palm log roofs.

Al Jahili Fort: In 1955, after its older buildings had fallen into disrepair, Sheikh Shakhbut offered Al Jahili Fort to the Trucial Oman Levies, renamed the Trucial Oman Scouts in 1956. Military use continued until the fort passed to the Union Defence Force in 1971.

Al Jahili Fort: Al Jahili Fort was restored from 1986 to 1989. The restoration created a single large courtyard, now used for classical music concerts and other public events, and added the present monumental entrance flanked by large towers.

Al Jahili Fort: Al Jahili Fort was conserved and developed as a visitor attraction in 2007, with an information centre and permanent and temporary exhibition spaces. Further conservation work in 2013 included building the north gate of the nineteenth century enclosure, based on archaeological evidence and historic photographs.
Al Jahili Fort: The Al Jahili Fort conservation project won the Terra Award at Terra Lyon 2016, the 12th World Congress on Earthen Architectures.
Al Jahili Fort: Al Jahili Fort uses a network of chilled water pipes laid beneath the mud plaster to cool the rooms around its arcaded gallery, when summer temperatures in Al Ain can reach 50°C.

Al Jahili Fort: At Al Jahili Fort, the north wing of the courtyard has a permanent exhibition of black and white photographs by the traveller Wilfred Thesiger, entitled 'Bin London and Freedom of the Desert'. The west wing is used for temporary exhibitions. The south wing has an information centre for visitors to the fort and to Al Ain, a bookshop and a majlis.

Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum, also called Al Ain National Museum, was founded in 1969 by Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan to showcase the archaeology and history of Al Ain. It is the oldest museum in the UAE and its first purpose-built museum.
Al Ain National Museum: From 1969 to 1970, a temporary exhibition was shown in Sultan Fort while the purpose-built museum was being constructed. Al Ain Museum was inaugurated on 2 November 1971.
Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum is east of Al Ain Oasis, in the historic district once known as Haret Al Hosn.

Al Ain National Museum: The collections and exhibitions of Al Ain Museum trace human life in the Al Ain region from the Palaeolithic period to the 20th century. They highlight developments such as the ancient aflaj irrigation system and the customs and lifeways of the people who shaped this desert oasis.

Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum houses artefacts found at archaeological sites across the region, including flint tools and arrowheads from the sixth millennium BCE and gold, electrum and silver jewellery.

Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum has nine permanent galleries arranged by period and theme, plus a temporary exhibition space and a visible storage area. They run from the Palaeolithic period and the Neolithic to the Iron Age, through an archaeological tomb and the aflaj and wells, to the Late Pre-Islamic and Late Islamic periods and the mid-20th century.

Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum combines buildings from different periods: archaeological remains preserved where they were found beneath the galleries, the early twentieth-century Sultan Fort, the museum building from the 1970s (now considered modern heritage), and new contemporary galleries.

Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum has been renewed: its original 1970s building was restored, Sultan Fort was revitalized, and four new exhibition galleries were built, three of them around archaeological remains from the Iron Age to the Late Pre-Islamic period.

Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum reopened to the public on 24 October 2025 after an extensive redevelopment. The redeveloped museum was designed by Dabbagh Architects, now spans more than 8,000 square metres, and keeps the original museum structure as part of its architecture.

Al Ain National Museum: Sultan Fort, also known as the Eastern Fort, was built in 1910 by Sheikh Sultan bin Zayed, the son of Sheikh Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan (Zayed the First), who ruled Abu Dhabi from 1922 to 1926. It is a well-preserved mudbrick fort with towers at three of its corners and a gate in its southern facade, and it stands within the grounds of Al Ain Museum, one of the museum's major attractions.

Al Ain National Museum: Sultan Fort lies at the eastern edge of Al Ain Oasis and once stood at the heart of the former village (hara) of Al Ain, which took its alternative name, Haret Al Hosn, from the fort.
Al Ain National Museum: Al Ain Museum is a key place for visitors to understand the wider network of UNESCO World Heritage Sites and cultural landmarks across Al Ain.
Al Ain Palace Museum: Al Ain Palace Museum is currently closed. It closed on July 1, 2024 for a renovation project.

Al Ain Palace Museum: Sheikh Zayed Palace Museum, also known as Al Ain Palace Museum, is in the palace of the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, Founding Father of the UAE. The palace was originally the residence of the UAE's ruling family and the Ruler's administrative centre.
Al Ain Palace Museum: Al Ain Palace Museum is on the western edge of Al Ain Oasis.
Al Ain Palace Museum: Al Ain Palace was built in 1937 and later extended by Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, who used it as his residence until 1966.
Al Ain Palace Museum: Al Ain Palace was converted into a museum in 1998 and opened to the public in 2001.

Al Ain Palace Museum: At Al Ain Palace Museum, visitors can experience the Emirati way of life in the 20th century and learn about the private and political life of the ruling family, especially that of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan.

Al Ain Palace Museum: Al Ain Palace has traditional ventilation structures and wide, long verandas that keep it cool in summer and shade the rooms from the sun. It was built with locally sourced materials, including clay, adobe, plaster stone and palm elements for the roofs, ceilings, doors and windows, and teak was added later in the renovation.

Al Ain Palace Museum: At Al Ain Palace, a distinctive internal gate decorated with verses from the Holy Qur'an leads to private rooms for guests and official delegations, and to rooms where councils met to issue directives on public services in the Eastern region of Abu Dhabi. The reception rooms for international delegations reflect the hospitality Sheikh Zayed and his family were known for.

Al Ain Palace Museum: Above the main entrance of Al Ain Palace is an upper majlis called Albarzah, which received important guests and provided shade in hot weather. The outdoor yard has the coffee room, from which Arabic coffee was served throughout the palace.

Al Ain Palace Museum: Al Ain Palace has a special section for Sheikh Zayed and his wife, Sheikha Fatima bint Mubarak Al Ketbi, on two floors. The ground floor was used by Sheikha Fatima to host women, and the upper floor was for Sheikh Zayed and his family. The palace also has a room where Sheikh Zayed's sons studied, which still has its original tables and blackboard, and a room for teaching the residents the Holy Qur'an and Hadith.

Al Ain Palace Museum: The renovation of Al Ain Palace added two new buildings. One houses the administration and displays gifts given to the museum by the local community, and the other shows the Al Nahyan family tree, with information about the country's rulers and their lineage. The towers added to the main entrance are similar to those of Al Jahili Fort.

Al Ain Palace Museum: A large tent in the Al Ain Palace Museum complex recalls the traditional tent that Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan used to receive guests, and reflects Bedouin tradition and Arab hospitality.

Al Ain Palace Museum: A courtyard at Al Ain Palace Museum has a Land Rover, similar to the ones Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan used on his travels across the desert to visit communities in the region.
Jebel Hafeet: Jebel Hafeet (also spelled Jebel Hafit or Jabal Hafit) is a mountain south of Al Ain, on the border between the UAE and Oman.
Jebel Hafeet: Jebel Hafeet is the highest peak in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi and the second highest in the UAE.

Jebel Hafeet: Visitors can reach the summit of Jebel Hafeet by car or motorbike or, with enough stamina, by bicycle. The views over Al Ain are popular at sunrise and sunset, and visiting during the day is recommended to take in the rocky mountain terrain.
Jebel Hafeet: At the top of Jebel Hafeet is the Mercure Jabal Hafit hotel, where visitors can take a break. Private operators run paid tours of the area from the hotel.
Jebel Hafeet: From the centre of Abu Dhabi, take the E22 Abu Dhabi-Al Ain Road to reach Jebel Hafeet.

Jebel Hafeet: Jebel Hafeet is home to some of the world's most threatened wildlife and the UAE's rarest plants. Threatened species there include Blanford's fox, Brandt's hedgehog, the Arabian tahr and the only concentration of globally threatened Egyptian vultures in the UAE.
Jebel Hafeet: Jebel Hafeet is the only place where the dwarf palm is found, one of the rarest plants in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi and on the Arabian Peninsula.
Jebel Hafeet: In February 2019, an Arabian caracal was recorded by camera trap in Jebel Hafeet National Park, the first sighting in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi since 1984.
Jebel Hafeet: Jebel Hafeet is suitable for families: children can look for wildlife and for plant and insect species, and there are views over Al Ain from the top.
Jebel Hafeet: Jebel Hafeet gave its name to the Hafit period of the Bronze Age, because of the cluster of beehive tombs found in its foothills.

Green Mubazzarah Hot Springs: Green Mubazzarah Hot Springs is a park of green lawns at the foot of Jebel Hafeet. Hot spring water from Jebel Hafeet runs through the park, forming a trail beside which visitors can walk.

Green Mubazzarah Hot Springs: Unlike typical cold mountain springs, the water at Green Mubazzarah is soothingly warm. It is especially inviting in the cooler months, when visitors walk beside the water and dip their feet in.
Green Mubazzarah Hot Springs: The Green Mubazzarah Chalets are next to the hot springs and offer stays for visitors who want to extend their visit.
Green Mubazzarah Hot Springs: Green Mubazzarah has a lake, formed by water from the hot springs.
Al Ain Zoo: Al Ain Zoo, also called Al Ain Wildlife Park, is at the foot of Jebel Hafeet and is home to over 4,000 animals.

Al Ain Zoo: Animals at Al Ain Zoo include the Arabian oryx, the big-horned Barbary sheep, rhinos, hippos, tigers and lions, as well as eland, gazelle, lechwe, the rare white lion and the Nubian giraffe. Transparent enclosures house both indigenous and exotic species.
Al Ain Zoo: Experiences at Al Ain Zoo include an up-close giraffe feeding, camel riding, the Elezba petting zoo, a walk-through lemur experience and a train tour of the wildlife area.

Al Ain Zoo: The Al Ain Zoo safari covers 217 hectares, where visitors get up close with lions, zebras and a range of other animals. Emirati wildlife experts guide the safari and offer personalised experiences.
Al Ain Zoo: Al Ain Zoo has a well-respected conservation and breeding programme that protects rare animals from extinction. The zoo is dedicated to conservation.
Al Ain Zoo: Al Ain Zoo has green public spaces for picnics, playgrounds, interactive play zones, and cafes and restaurants, which makes it a popular choice for families.
Al Ain Zoo: Visitors can pre-reserve a dinner next to the lions at the Al Ain Zoo safari.
Al Ain Zoo: The Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre is inside Al Ain Zoo.

Hili Archaeological Park: Hili Archaeological Park was developed to highlight the ancient monuments of Al Ain and make them easily accessible to visitors. It combines a public garden with an archaeological site.
Hili Archaeological Park: Hili Archaeological Park is in the north-east of Al Ain, on the road toward Dubai.
Hili Archaeological Park: Hili Archaeological Park is part of the UNESCO World Heritage property Cultural Sites of Al Ain (Hafit, Hili, Bidaa Bint Saud and Oases Areas), inscribed in 2011.

Hili Archaeological Park: Most of the monuments at Hili Archaeological Park are from the Umm an-Nar period, from about 2500 BCE to 2000 BCE. The period is named after the island near Abu Dhabi where remains of this culture were first found. The largest collection of tombs and buildings from this period in the UAE is at Hili.

Hili Archaeological Park: The centrepiece of Hili Archaeological Park is the Hili Grand Tomb, dating to about 2000 BCE. It is circular, up to 12 metres across and about 4 metres high, and was used to bury people from the surrounding settlements. It has two entrances decorated with engraved reliefs of human and animal figures.

Hili Archaeological Park: Besides tombs, Hili has Bronze Age and Iron Age villages, burial grounds, forts and agricultural infrastructure, within and just outside the park. A number of the Bronze Age structures inside the park are open to the public.
Hili Archaeological Park: Hili Site 8, one of the Bronze Age settlements at Hili, has the earliest known evidence of agriculture in the UAE, dating to about 3000 BCE, roughly 5,000 years ago.
Hili Archaeological Park: Artefacts from the Hili sites can be seen in the Al Ain National Museum.
Hili Archaeological Park: Hili Archaeological Park is chiefly a garden, with plants, fountains and a small children's play area. It is a popular place for international visitors and residents.
Wadi Adventure (Al Ain Adventure): Wadi Adventure, also called Al Ain Adventure Park, is a family-friendly adventure park at the foot of Jebel Hafeet.

Wadi Adventure (Al Ain Adventure): Wadi Adventure has the Middle East's first man-made whitewater rafting channels, 1,100 metres long, for rafting and kayaking. It also has surfing, wakeboarding, a swimming pool and a splash pool.
Wadi Adventure (Al Ain Adventure): The aerial adventure course at Wadi Adventure has an 18-obstacle, two-level airpark, a 1,200-metre zip line, a vertical climb line and a 14-metre-high giant swing.

Wadi Adventure (Al Ain Adventure): Other activities at Wadi Adventure include the jacuzzis at Oasis Island, Aqua Island (a floating obstacle course for kids and adults), off-road 4x4 tracks, hiking trails and obstacle courses.
Wadi Adventure (Al Ain Adventure): Visitors can stay overnight at Wadi Adventure in its eco-lodges or in the Campers Village.
Hili Fun City: Hili Fun City opened in 1985 and was the Arabian Gulf region's first theme park. It is near Hazza Bin Zayed Stadium.
Hili Fun City: Hili Fun City is a modernised family entertainment park with attractions for all ages, an amphitheatre, and picnic and play areas.
Hili Fun City: Hili Fun City has an ice rink.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: Qasr Al Muwaiji, also called Muwaiji Fort, is a historic mudbrick fort on the western approach to Al Ain city, next to Al Muwaiji Oasis. It is a fine example of early 20th century mudbrick architecture and has played an important role in the history of the UAE.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: Qasr Al Muwaiji was built in the early 20th century, during the rule of Sheikh Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan (Zayed the First, who ruled Abu Dhabi from 1855 to 1909), by his son Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: Qasr Al Muwaiji is a square enclosure measuring 65 by 65 metres, with square towers projecting from the north-west and south-east corners. Its gate is set slightly off-centre in the southern wall, facing Al Muwaiji Oasis, the smallest and most westerly oasis of Al Ain.
Qasr Al Muwaiji: Qasr Al Muwaiji was used as a diwan (a council or seat of governance) and as a place for the community to gather.
Qasr Al Muwaiji: In 1946, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan was appointed Ruler's Representative in Al Ain and moved to Qasr Al Muwaiji, which became his diwan and his family home.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the eldest son of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan and the late President of the UAE, was born at Qasr Al Muwaiji in 1948 and spent much of his youth there, learning from his father.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan made many additions to Qasr Al Muwaiji as its importance as the seat of government in the region grew. He added new diwan buildings and kitchens, expanded the guest accommodation for the increasing number of visitors, and enlarged the fort's mosque.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: When Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan became Ruler of Abu Dhabi in 1966, he and his son Sheikh Khalifa moved to Abu Dhabi. From the 1970s Qasr Al Muwaiji went through several phases of restoration, ending in a major regeneration project that made it an important public space in Al Ain again.
Qasr Al Muwaiji: Qasr Al Muwaiji and Al Muwaiji Oasis are key components of the UNESCO World Heritage property Cultural Sites of Al Ain, inscribed in 2011.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: Qasr Al Muwaiji has an exhibition in a modern glass building in the courtyard of the palace, telling the story of the palace and its inhabitants. It shows the connection between the palace and the members of Abu Dhabi's ruling family, from Sheikh Zayed the First down to Sheikh Khalifa.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: The main focus of the Qasr Al Muwaiji exhibition is the life and achievements of Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan. It follows his preparation for leadership under his father, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan, and then his accomplishments as President: investing in his people, extending the UAE's regional and international influence, and leading the nation toward a better future.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: The Qasr Al Muwaiji exhibition also traces the history of the fort from the earliest archaeological evidence to today. It covers the fort's role in hosting visiting travellers, the importance of water to its survival, and its significance as a family home, seat of power and focus for the Al Ain community.

Qasr Al Muwaiji: Al Muwaiji Oasis, near Qasr Al Muwaiji, is the smallest oasis in Al Ain, with about 21,000 palm trees. Its falaj irrigation system uses ground-level and underground canals to bring water from the nearby mountains, and the fort's grounds have been used over the years for date palm cultivation.
Qasr Al Muwaiji: Wilfred Thesiger visited Al Ain in the late 1940s, during his travels across the Empty Quarter. He met Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan and stayed with him at Qasr Al Muwaiji.

Al Ain Camel Market: Al Ain Camel Market is a traditional market on Zayed Bin Sultan Street, about 15 kilometres from downtown Al Ain. Traders buy and sell camels, goats and sheep there, and it gives visitors a glimpse of traditional Emirati and Bedouin culture.
Al Ain Camel Market: Trading at Al Ain Camel Market is busiest in the mornings, and herded animals can usually be seen throughout the day.

Al Ain Camel Market: At Al Ain Camel Market, visitors can see young Arabian camels that may grow up to be racers and adult camels suited to breeding, and watch locals arrive in pickups loaded with goats and sheep to haggle.
Al Ain Camel Market: Al Ain Camel Market is a working market, so visits must be planned in advance and are supervised by market staff, to keep the visit safe and organised.
Al Ain Camel Market: Visitors to Al Ain Camel Market should not touch the camels without permission and are advised to dress modestly and respectfully.

Al Ain Camel Market: Camels have long been important to Emirati culture because of their strength and dependability. Bedouins used them to cross the desert, and their milk, wool and meat were, and still are, widely used. Camels also take part in races and beauty contests.

Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): The Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque, also known as the Al Ain Grand Mosque, the Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Grand Mosque or the Sheikh Khalifa Mosque, is the largest mosque in Al Ain and one of the largest in the UAE.

Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): The Al Ain Grand Mosque opened to the public on 12 April 2021. It is named after Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the late Ruler of Abu Dhabi and President of the UAE, who held the presidency from November 2004 until his death in May 2022.
Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): The Al Ain Grand Mosque can hold more than 20,000 worshippers in its indoor and outdoor spaces.
Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): The built-up area of the Al Ain Grand Mosque is 15,684 square metres.
Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): The Al Ain Grand Mosque has four minarets, each about 60 metres high, inspired by the Great Mosque of Samarra.

Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): The huge dome of the Al Ain Grand Mosque covers the main prayer hall and is decorated with verses from the Quran. It is 86 metres across on the outside.
Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): Next to the Al Ain Grand Mosque stands a mosque about 1,000 years old, from the Islamic Golden Age.
Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Mosque (Al Ain Grand Mosque): Al Ain may be the location of the oldest mosque in the UAE, which is in the premises of the Sheikh Khalifa Mosque.
Al Qattara Arts Centre: Al Qattara Arts Centre plays a unique role in Al Ain's artistic and cultural scene. It is a place to create art as well as to see it.

Al Qattara Arts Centre: Al Qattara Arts Centre was established in 2011 as a venue where culture and the creative arts can be studied, practiced and developed. It is also one of Al Ain's leading venues for events and exhibitions that explore the region's cultural heritage.
Al Qattara Arts Centre: The art gallery at Al Qattara Arts Centre displays work by expatriate and Emirati artists.

Al Qattara Arts Centre: Al Qattara Arts Centre has studios for art classes. The Dry Studio is a classroom for music and handicrafts, the Wet Studio offers drawing and painting lessons, and there is also a Pottery Studio and a Calligraphy Studio.

Al Qattara Arts Centre: Al Qattara Arts Centre is a redevelopment of the former Bin Ati Al Darmaki House, a traditional mud brick tower and residence. It was designed in the regional architectural style and blends in with the modern heritage buildings around it.

Al Qattara Arts Centre: Al Qattara Archaeological Basement, at Al Qattara Arts Centre, is a permanent exhibition on the archaeology of the oases of Al Ain, using finds from the site and a range of media. Excavations during the creation of the centre revealed a five-metre sequence of archaeological layers spanning the Late Islamic period to the Iron Age, and the Iron Age industrial installations from the earliest phase are on display there.

Al Qattara Arts Centre: Among the key objects in Al Qattara Archaeological Basement is a lion figurine from the Iron Age II period (1100-600 BCE). It probably once formed part of a large pottery vessel and is one of the finest decorated Iron Age ceramic figurines ever found in the UAE.

Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre: The Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre (SZDLC) is inside Al Ain Zoo. It is an educational facility that teaches visitors about the UAE's natural environment through interactive exhibits, multimedia and visual materials.

Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre: The Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre has five interactive galleries: the Sheikh Zayed Tribute Hall, Abu Dhabi's Desert Over Time, Abu Dhabi's Living World, People of the Desert, and Looking to the Future.

Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre: Public tours at the Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre are led by trained Emirati cultural guides. They take visitors on a journey through time, with stories and movies about the past, present and future of the UAE's environment, encouraging people to reconsider their relationship with the environment, connect with it and adopt more sustainable lifestyles.

Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre: The Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre is a building with multiple levels. Its exhibits include immersive environments, audio-visual interactive exhibits, stylised sculptures and models, specimen collections, graphics and a large-scale theatre.

Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre: The Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre building has LEED Platinum certification. It was the first building in the UAE to earn a five-pearl sustainability rating at the design and construction stage, under standards set by the Abu Dhabi Urban Planning Council.
Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre: The Sheikh Zayed Desert Learning Centre also has a large library of environmental resources and publications.

Souq Al Qattara: Souq Al Qattara, also called Al Qattara Heritage Souq, is a restored traditional market in Al Ain that celebrates Emirati heritage. It is near Al Qattara Oasis and Al Qattara Arts Centre.
Souq Al Qattara: The historic structure of Souq Al Qattara was built in the 1930s and restored in 1976. It has thick mud walls, a palm-frond roof and ventilation systems that suit desert living.
Souq Al Qattara: At Souq Al Qattara, visitors can browse for souvenirs, spices, perfumes and handicrafts, and enjoy gahwa (Arabic coffee) with dates or local sweets such as luqaimat.

Souq Al Qattara: Souq Al Qattara hosts the annual Traditional Handicrafts Festival, which showcases artisans from across the UAE. It includes live demonstrations of crafts such as palm-frond work, pottery and Sadu and Talli weaving, folk performances and cultural programmes, and visitors can buy unique products.

Al Ain Racecourse (Equestrian, Shooting & Golf Club): The Al Ain Racecourse, also called the Al Ain Grandstand and Racecourse, is a major hub for racing enthusiasts across the UAE. It belongs to the Al Ain Equestrian, Shooting and Golf Club (AESGC), which is the sports headquarters in Al Ain and the region.

Al Ain Racecourse (Equestrian, Shooting & Golf Club): The Al Ain Racecourse opened for its inaugural racing season on 31 January 2014. It is best known for the Al Ain Mile Stakes (Group 3) and the Al Ain Marathon Series, which includes a final leg of 5,100 metres.
Al Ain Racecourse (Equestrian, Shooting & Golf Club): The Al Ain Racecourse has the largest racetrack in the UAE, at 2,500 metres, with a natural sand and dirt surface.
Al Ain Racecourse (Equestrian, Shooting & Golf Club): The historic grandstand at the Al Ain Racecourse holds more than 4,000 spectators, and the total capacity of the venue is above 10,000.
Al Ain Racecourse (Equestrian, Shooting & Golf Club): The Al Ain Racecourse has a rail-side restaurant inside the adjoining golf club, open to horsemen, patrons, travellers and guests.

Jebel Hafeet Mountain Road (Cycling Climb): The road up Jebel Hafeet is one of the most iconic cycling routes in Al Ain, a challenging hill climb with views of the surrounding desert and mountains. The final ascent is steep, and the reward is a panoramic view and an exciting descent.
Jebel Hafeet Mountain Road (Cycling Climb): The road to the summit of Jebel Hafeet can be driven by car, ridden by motorbike or, with enough stamina, cycled.

Al Ain Cycling Track: The Al Ain Cycling Track is a well-maintained, flat, paved route of about 23 kilometres through Al Ain, passing through parks, gardens and historical sites. It is a good option for a leisurely ride.
Al Ain Cycling Track: The Al Ain Cycling Track is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and has an onsite bicycle rental shop.
Al Ain Cycling Track: The Al Ain Cycling Track hosts several cycling events throughout the year, including the Al Ain Cycle Track Classic.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: Jebel Hafeet Desert Park, also called Jebel Hafeet National Park or Mezyad Desert Park, occupies a nine-kilometre stretch at the foot of Jebel Hafeet. It aims to preserve the area's wildlife, plants, environment and geology while attracting tourists, and it includes the Hafit tombs, Mezyad Fort and nearby oases.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: At Jebel Hafeet Desert Park, visitors can hike, mountain bike, or ride a horse or camel, and discover archaeological and historical remains that range from the Neolithic period 8,000 years ago to the 5,000-year-old Hafit tombs. The park is family-friendly.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: More than 500 ancient burial tombs, about 5,000 years old, have been found in the foothills of Jebel Hafeet, marking the start of the Bronze Age in the UAE. The Hafit tombs were excavated by Danish archaeologists in 1959, at the request of the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan.
Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: Jebel Hafeet Desert Park organises guided hikes to see the Hafit tombs.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: Jebel Hafeet Desert Park and the Hafit tombs are part of the UNESCO World Heritage property Cultural Sites of Al Ain (Hafit, Hili, Bidaa Bint Saud and Oases Areas), inscribed in 2011.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: The Hafit tombs were built over about 500 years, between 3000 and 2500 BCE. The early inhabitants of the Al Ain region chose the northern and eastern slopes of Jebel Hafeet for them, and the most prominent group is a necropolis along the eastern foothills. Other tombs lie along hills and ridges between Jebel Hafeet and Al Ain city, about 20 kilometres to the north.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: Each domed Hafit tomb, often called a beehive tomb, has a single round or oval chamber about 2 to 3 metres wide, built of uncut or rough-cut local rock. Ring walls around the chamber rise 3 to 4 metres and slope inwards to form a dome.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: The Hafit tombs have narrow entrances, and each held the remains of between two and five people. This is different from the later Umm an-Nar tombs, in which hundreds of people were buried together.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: Finds from the Hafit tombs show trade links with ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq), Iran and the Indus Valley (modern-day Pakistan and India), and the importance of maritime trade across the Arabian Gulf. They include ceramic vessels, copper artefacts, imported Mesopotamian pottery, small blue-green tubular beads thought to have been imported, and beads of local stone shaped as trapezoids or squares.

Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: Spearheads and daggers from the second millennium BCE (2000 to 1000 BCE) and soapstone vessels were also found in the Hafit tombs, which shows that the tombs were reused. The reuse became widespread in the Iron Age (1000 to 600 BCE).
Jebel Hafeet Desert Park & Tombs: Jebel Hafeet Desert Park also offers overnight stays, from camping under the stars to glamping tents and authentic Bedouin-style tents.

Al Jahili Park: Al Jahili Park is one of the prominent parks in Al Ain, a key recreational destination with extensive green spaces and integrated facilities that attract families and visitors throughout the year.

Al Towayya Park: Al Towayya Park is one of the prominent parks in Al Ain, a key recreational destination with extensive green spaces and integrated facilities that attract families and visitors throughout the year.
Jebel Hafeet Park (Mubazzarah area): Jebel Hafeet Park, in the Mubazzarah area, is set against Jebel Hafeet and shows the charm of Al Ain's lush green oasis.
Jebel Hafeet Park (Mubazzarah area): The expansive lawns of Jebel Hafeet Park are an inviting backdrop for picnics and barbecues. There are no tickets to enter the park.
Jebel Hafeet Park (Mubazzarah area): At Jebel Hafeet Park, visitors can take a dip in the hot springs with the mountain breeze, and adventurous visitors can find secluded pools nearby.

Al Aankah Fort (Al A'ankah / Alanka): Al A'ankah Fort is a historic fort in Al Ain, in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi. Sheikh Saeed bin Tahnoun commissioned it in the second half of the 19th century to protect the lands of the Al Nahyan family, particularly along the road between Abu Dhabi and Al Ain.
Al Aankah Fort (Al A'ankah / Alanka): The name Al A'ankah is linked to the red sands of the surrounding area, and it may also refer to how difficult the fort was to reach or conquer.
Al Ain public parks: Al Ain City has 55 public parks and 224 small residential parks spread across its neighbourhoods, so recreational and community facilities are close to where people live.

Al Ain public parks: Prominent parks in Al Ain include Al Jahili Park, Al Ain Oasis Green Park, Al Towayya Park, Al Aini Park and Hili Archaeological Park. They are key recreational destinations for families and visitors throughout the year.
Al Ain public parks: Nineteen parks in Al Ain City received the 2025 Green Flag Award, an international benchmark for park management, sustainability and service quality.
Al Ain: Al Ain (Arabic: ٱلْعَيْن, romanized: Al-ʿAyn, lit. 'The Spring') is a city in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, and the seat of the administrative division of the Al Ain Region.
Al Ain: Al Ain is the largest inland city in the Emirates, the fourth-largest city (after Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Sharjah), and the second-largest in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi.

Al Ain Climate and Geography: Al Ain is known as the "Garden City" of Abu Dhabi, the UAE or the Gulf, due to its greenery, particularly with regard to the city's oases, parks, tree-lined avenues and decorative roundabouts, with strict height controls on new buildings, to no more than seven floors.

Al Ain Climate and Geography: Road distances between Al Ain, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah: Al Ain to Abu Dhabi is about 155 km, Al Ain to Dubai is about 130 km, Al Ain to Sharjah is about 148 km, and Abu Dhabi to Dubai is about 139 km.

Al Ain Climate and Geography: Al Ain is right next to Oman: the Omani town of Al Buraimi borders Al Ain directly on its east. Sharjah is about 148 km from Al Ain by road, so Oman's border is much closer to Al Ain than Sharjah is.
Al Ain Climate and Geography: Al Ain's eastern region covers an area of approximately 13,100 km2 (5,100 sq mi).

Al Ain Climate and Geography: Al Ain city is bordered to the east by the Omani town of Al Buraimi. Oman lies to the east of Al Ain, Dubai and Sharjah to the north of Al Ain, Abu Dhabi to the west of Al Ain and the Empty Quarter desert and Saudi Arabia to the south of Al Ain.
Al Ain Climate and Geography: The topography of Al Ain is unique and varies as one travels to the east.
Al Ain Climate and Geography: Al Ain city has a hot desert climate, featuring long, extremely hot summers and warm winters.
Al Ain Climate and Geography: Low humidity in Al Ain, particularly during the summers, makes it a popular destination for many people during this time of the year.
Al Ain Climate and Geography: To the south of Al Ain, near Oman, there is the man-made Lake Zakher, which resulted from the release of waste water from desalination plants.
Al Ain Climate and Geography: In Al Ain, to the east of Jebel Hafeet, lies the area of Mezyad, which has a border crossing with Oman, and is where the historic Mezyad Fort is located.

Al Ain Economy: Al Ain is an important services centre for a wide area extending into Oman. Besides its major shopping centres, Al Ain has traditional souqs for fruit and vegetables and livestock, along the road which leads to Mezyad.

Al Ain Economy: Al Ain social and governmental infrastructure include well-equipped medical facilities including the teaching hospital at Tawam, Al Ain International Airport, and military training areas.
Places of Worship: In 2021, the Sheikh Khalifa Grand Mosque became the biggest mosque in Al Ain, as well as one of the largest mosques in the UAE.
Places of Worship: Al Ain has a Roman Catholic parish, St. Mary's Catholic Church.
Transportation: Al Ain is connected to Dubai and Al Faqa' in the north by the Dubai-Al Ain Road.
Transportation: Al Ain is also connected by road to Abu Dhabi in the west, and to Al Qu'a and Mezyad.
Transportation: The southern border area of Mezyad lies on the road to Dhank, Ibri and Nizwa in Oman.

Tourism and Recreation: Al Ain is developing as a tourist destination, as the dry desert air makes it a welcome retreat from the coastal humidity of the larger cities. Many Emirati nationals in Abu Dhabi have holiday houses in Al Ain, making it a popular weekend destination for families from the capital city.

Tourism and Recreation: Al Ain's attractions include the Al Ain National Museum, the Sheikh Zayed Palace Museum (also known as the Al Ain Palace Museum), several restored forts and the Hili Archaeological Park, which dates back to the Bronze Age.

Tourism and Recreation: Jebel Hafeet dominates the surrounding area of Al Ain. Visitors to Al Ain popularly go to the mineral springs at Green Mubazzarah, at the base of Jebel Hafeet, and drive to the top of Jebel Hafeet at sunset.

Tourism and Recreation: Other attractions in Al Ain include Al Ain Zoo, an amusement park named "Hili Fun City", many well-maintained parks popular with families in the summer evenings, and a heritage village.
Tourism and Recreation: Wadi Adventure, also known as Al Ain Adventure, opened in 2012 near Jebel Hafeet and provides a range of water-based activities including surfing, kayaking and rafting.

Tourism and Recreation: Jebel Hafeet and the nearby 'beehive' tombs are part of what is known as "Jebel Hafeet Desert Park" or "Mezyad Desert Park", which is meant to preserve the nature and geology of the area, besides attracting tourists.

Tourism and Recreation: Al Ain has five major malls: Al Ain Mall in the town centre, Al Jimi Mall in the Al Jimi District, Bawadi Mall in the Al Khrair District, Remal Mall in the Sanaiya district, and Hili Mall in the Hili District. Most commercial activity is centred in and around the town centre.
Tourism and Recreation: Al Jimi Mall has an IKEA store built into the mall. Bawadi Mall opened in 2009 in the Al Khrair area.
Tourism and Recreation: Spending time in coffee shops and shisha cafes is a popular pastime for Emiratis and expatriates alike in Al Ain. There are many cafes in Al Ain, ranging in size and quality.

Tourism and Recreation: Alcohol in Al Ain, which is in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, is sold in licensed shops and served in licensed venues such as hotels, restaurants and clubs, and must be consumed in those venues or in a private home. Public drinking is prohibited, the minimum age is 21, and rules can change, so check the current regulations.

Buraimi Oasis: The region of Al Ain and Al Buraimi, together known as the Buraimi Oasis, is of cultural and historical importance. The area witnessed events relevant to the history of Islam during the Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid eras, similar to Dibba and Ras Al-Khaimah.

Buraimi Oasis: Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the founder of the United Arab Emirates, spent considerable time of his life at the Buraimi Oasis, from approximately 1927 until he became the Ruler of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi in 1966.
Buraimi Oasis: Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan was born at Qasr Al Hosn, Abu Dhabi, in 1918, and was moved and raised in Al Ain in 1926 after the death of his father.

Al Ain prehistory: Part of the historically important Western Hajar region, the area of Al Ain has been inhabited for nearly 8,000 years, with archaeological sites showing human settlement at places like Rumailah, Hili and Jebel Hafeet.

Al Ain prehistory: The early Hafit culture built "beehive" tombs for their dead and engaged in hunting and gathering in the area of Al Ain. The oases of Al Ain provided water for early farms until the modern age.

Al Ain prehistory: In the 1950s, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan discovered the tombs in the Western Hajar region and brought this to the attention of a Danish team, leading to an excavation at the tombs in 1959.

Al Ain World Heritage status: In the 2000s, the Abu Dhabi Authority for Culture & Heritage lobbied for UNESCO World Heritage Site recognition for Al Ain. In 2011, Al Ain became the first World Heritage Site in the UAE to be recognized by UNESCO.

Al Ain rulers and tribes: Al Ain was originally within the area of influence of the Dhawahir, a Bedouin tribe who settled Dhahirah before Buraimi. A later wave of settlers, the Na'im, have long had an uneasy relationship with the Dhawahir, and the two tribes were frequently in dispute.

Al Ain rulers and tribes: A number of interests jostled for influence over the tribes of Buraimi, including the Sultan of Muscat, the Wahhabis (who had made a number of incursions) and the Sheikhs of the Trucial States, particularly the Bani Yas of Abu Dhabi, who acquired large tracts of land, principally from the Dhawahir.

Al Ain rulers and tribes: Sheikh Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan, known as 'Zayed the Great', cemented Abu Dhabi's suzerainty over Al Ain. A strong and charismatic leader, he took the Dhawahir's main settlement, 'Ain Dhawahir (the original name of Al Ain), when the tribe rebelled against him in 1877. He built a fort, one of a number of fortifications established by the various interests vying for control over the oasis, to underline his dominion over the oasis. He also established a wali, appointing a member of the Dhawahir as his headman.

Buraimi Dispute: An ongoing dispute between Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Oman led to the Buraimi Dispute, a series of incidents which saw a Saudi armed force enter the oasis. Forces from the Trucial Oman Scouts, as well as the army of Muscat-Oman, arrived to recapture the oasis. With British intervention, the Saudi forces surrendered, leaving the oasis back in the hands of Abu Dhabi and Oman.

Al Ain modern history: Following independence in 1971, Al Ain experienced rapid growth and investment as part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, quickly becoming larger and more successful than Oman's Al Buraimi.
Al Ain modern history: In 1972, Oman and Abu Dhabi agreed on the final borders dividing Al Buraimi and Al Ain.

Al Ain modern history: Until the death of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan in 2004, Al Ain's municipal code forbade construction of buildings over four stories, with the exceptions of the Hilton (now Radisson Blu), Danat Al Ain Resort, and Rotana hotels.

Al Ain archaeology: Bronze Age burial sites in Al Ain often re-used materials from earlier burials. For instance, the Wadi Suq communal tomb at Qattara Oasis is thought to have been constructed from stones recovered from previous Umm Al Nar burials.

Al Ain archaeology: Finds at Qattara Oasis include Wadi Suq era chlorite jugs and bowls and late Bronze Age short swords and daggers. Artefacts recovered also include carnelian jewellery, often associated by UAE historians with trading links to the Indus Valley.

Al Ain archaeology: A find of particular interest from Qattara Oasis is a Bronze Age pendant discovered in the 1970s depicting a double-bodied or entwined pair of horned animals. Made from electrum, an alloy of silver and gold, the motif is found repeated in a number of Bronze Age sites in the UAE.

Al Ain archaeology: Iron Age finds in and around Al Ain include aflaj (underground water channels) in Bidaa bint Saud, Al Ain and Buraimi, which have been placed several centuries prior to the qanats of the Achaemenid Empire, which had previously been credited with the innovation.

Dhawahir tribe: The Dhawahir tribe numbered 4,500 and consisted of three subsections: the Daramikah, who populated Hili, Mutared and Qattara; the Jawabir in Al Ain; and the Bani Saad, who lived in Jimi. The community stayed in the villages for the summer date season and in winter would move throughout the Trucial States.
